Photo by Radek Mica / AFP via Getty Images. Tuesday, November 17, 2026 - Iran: Iran targets U.S. military facilities in Bahrain for third time. Qatar announces new talks with Tehran. Iran's Navy says five tankers struck naval mines near Hormuz. Tehran warns NYT report linking dams to missile sites could pave way for attacks on civilian infrastructure. CNN goes Judith Miller: U.S. intelligence warns of suspected Iranian dirty bomb plot, Iran rejects claim as "fabricated." Only 31% of Americans support U.S. war on Iran. Iran claims capture of ninth U.S. drone over Qeshm Island; shoots down another. Palestine: Israeli forces kill two Palestinians in Gaza attacks. Israeli airstrike hits near UN fuel convoy in Gaza. Israeli settlers kill 72-year-old Palestinian woman, wound 10 others in Jericho attack. Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers injure eight Palestinians as forces demolish homes. UK sanctions eight Israeli settlement firms and group blocking Gaza aid. EU sanctions Gaza outlet over alleged Hamas fundraising. Yemen: Ansarallah reports nine wounded in Sana'a airstrike. Saudi-backed forces reinforce defenses around Aden amid Ansarallah advance. Saudi Arabia replaces Yemen coalition commander following withdrawal from Bab al-Mandab. Lebanon: Israeli forces continue ceasefire violations across southern Lebanon. U.S. envoy urges Hezbollah to disarm voluntarily as UN peacekeeping mandate nears expiration. U.S.: Hakeem Jeffries moves for recorded leadership vote as Ayanna Pressley flirts with bid. Permitting reform clears major Senate hurdle. Forensic scientist argues that evidence strongly points to Epstein homicide. GOP Rep. DesJarlais concedes his reelection race in Tennessee. Rep. Ro Khanna suggests $1,700 refund checks for every American to cover costs of Iran War. White House tells agencies federal employees "must obtain approval" before agreeing to testify before Congress. Commerce and Justice Departments defend handling of Megaspeed. Major software outage at Chase Bank. International: UN report: Drone strikes account for over 80% of civilians killed in Sudan in first half of 2026. Prominent Bahraini human rights activist dies at 62. Five European countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. Nigeria's military says it is receiving U.S. intelligence and satellite help in strikes on militants. Mongolian president announces his resignation after accusations of corruption. Costa Rican journalist shot dead in capital. Russian strikes two Kyiv bridges hours after Ukraine holds new talks on ending the war. This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday - Friday Iran Iran targets U.S. military facilities in Bahrain for third time: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Tuesday it launched a drone attack targeting a U.S. radar system at Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain, in what it described as a response to repeated violations of Iranian airspace by U.S. military drones. AFP reported explosions in the Bahraini capital, Manama, after the Interior Ministry warned residents of an unspecified danger. U.S. Central Command that the radar system had been hit, saying multiple Iranian drones launched toward Bahrain were intercepted without damaging U.S. equipment or injuring American personnel. Qatar announces new talks with Tehran: Qatar said Tuesday that mediation efforts to end the U.S.-Iran conflict were continuing, announcing plans to meet Iranian officials in the coming hours. "Today's meeting with the Iranian side will take place as part of mediation efforts and an exchange of views on the current proposals," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said during a press briefing in Doha. Warning that "any escalation on the ground poses a challenge to mediation efforts," Al-Ansari urged both sides to exercise restraint and avoid further escalation. Iran 's Navy says five tankers struck naval mines near Hormuz: Another tanker and sustained severe damage on Tuesday after striking a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the reported number of tankers damaged in the past 24 hours to five, according to Iran's Navy. The Navy claimed the vessel was traveling through a "prohibited" area with its navigation systems switched off. Separately, Iran's IRGC Navy said a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil and a liquefied petroleum gas carrier had struck naval mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. It remains unclear whether the two vessels are included in the Navy's reported total. Tehran warns NYT report linking dams to missile sites could pave way for attacks on civilian infrastructure: Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf charged The New York Times of laying the groundwork for further U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iranian civilian infrastructure after the newspaper published an suggesting that some of the country's dams and water transfer projects may have been built partly to support underground missile facilities. The report cited researchers who found that the locations of numerous dams closely overlapped with suspected missile sites targeted in U.S. and Israeli airstrikes this year, although the researchers acknowledged that any connection remains speculative and that many dams serve essential civilian needs. "Prepping the next round on civilian infra," Ghalibaf on X. "New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a U.S. or Israeli base is dual-use. We'll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly." CNN goes Judith Miller: U.S. intelligence warns of suspected Iranian dirty bomb plot, Iran rejects claim as "fabricated": U.S. intelligence Iran may be developing plans for a possible dirty bomb or chemical weapons attack targeting senior Trump administration officials in Washington, D.C., CNN reported Tuesday. Sources said the intelligence identified specific locations and targets but stressed that there was no evidence Tehran had decided to carry out an attack. The White House said there were "no credible threats to the homeland." Asked about the report, President Donald Trump warned that Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before" if it attacked Washington. Iran's UN mission rejected the chemical weapons allegations as "false and fabricated," while Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei accused those who started the war of attempting to manufacture justification for further attacks. Days earlier, Israel Hayom reported that Israel's Mossad had warned the CIA of an alleged Iranian drone plot targeting Trump and senior U.S. officials. Only 31% of Americans support U.S. war on Iran: Just 31% of American adults support the U.S. war on Iran, according to a new . Trump's approval rating stands at 32%, near the lowest level of his presidency, after falling to a record low of 31% in mid-October. In an interview with Fox News, Vice President JD Vance acknowledged the war's political consequences, citing "the higher gas prices, the higher energy prices," after previously linking the conflict to Republican losses in the midterm elections. "People who want it to become a forever war, they can attack me all they want to because we signed up to not do this," Vance said, accusing some "neoconservatives" of wanting the U.S. to "stay there forever." Vance insisted there was "no daylight" between him and Trump, despite the president recently saying he had told Vance that the U.S. did not need a deal with Iran. Iran claims capture of ninth U.S. drone over Qeshm Island; shoots down another: The IRGC Tuesday that it had captured another U.S. MQM-170 drone through an electronic warfare operation over southern Qeshm Island, bringing the total number of such drones it claims to have seized to nine. The IRGC said its specialists took control of the aircraft and brought it down intact. Iran's army separately said it shot down a U.S.-made LUCAS attack drone over Hormuz, according to state broadcaster IRIB. Palestine Israeli forces kill two Palestinians in Gaza attacks: Israeli forces shot and killed a Palestinian man and wounded several others in the Al-Jaafrawi area east of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza on Tuesday, according to WAFA. Separately, a Palestinian succumbed to injuries sustained in an earlier Israeli airstrike in Jabalia, northern Gaza. Israeli airstrike hits near UN fuel convoy in Gaza: An Israeli airstrike struck "very close" to a UN-led fuel convoy in Rafah, southern Gaza, on Sunday, to the United Nations. UN deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq warned that strikes near humanitarian vehicles, particularly those carrying fuel, expose aid workers to "unacceptable risks," adding that the UN had raised the incident with Israeli authorities. Haq called for increased humanitarian funding and faster entry of essential supplies restricted by Israel. Earlier this month, a senior Palestinian source involved in negotiations Drop Site that Israel had ordered a complete halt to aid and commercial shipments entering Gaza from Egypt, warning that "fuel and gas come entirely through this route," which handles approximately 50-60 trucks daily. Israeli settlers kill 72-year-old Palestinian woman, wound 10 others in Jericho attack: Israeli settlers a 72-year-old Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other Palestinians during an overnight attack on Ein Al-Duyuk Al-Tahta, west of Jericho in the occupied West Bank, according to WAFA. During the attack, settlers surrounded Palestinian homes while Israeli forces raided the village and closed three entrances to Jericho. Israeli soldiers also severely beat WAFA photojournalist Suleiman Abu Surour while he was covering the attack, leaving him with fractures and bruises. Soldiers detained him for six hours and confiscated his phone before releasing him. Later Tuesday, Israeli forces informed Fheidat's family that they were prohibited from holding a funeral for her in the village. The attack came nearly two weeks after settlers seized eight homes in the village at gunpoint and continued occupying them. Read Katrine Dige Houm øller's report for Drop Site on the settlers' seizure of homes in Jericho . Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers injure eight Palestinians as forces demolish homes: Bethlehem: An Israeli settler drove a vehicle into a group of Palestinians gathered near a traffic accident in Tuqu, southeast of Bethlehem, on Monday, injuring eight people, according to WAFA. Hebron: Israeli forces three homes sheltering 21 Palestinians along with two livestock sheds and two water wells in the Al-Deirat and Al-Duwarat areas east of Yatta on Tuesday. Tubas: Israeli forces greenhouses in Bardala in the northern Jordan Valley. Settlers also destroyed agricultural irrigation networks near Ein Al-Beida. Occupied East Jerusalem: Settlers a new settlement outpost near Palestinian homes in the Al-Hayy area outside Mikhmas, northeast of occupied East Jerusalem. UK sanctions eight Israeli settlement firms and group blocking Gaza aid: The UK new sanctions on Tuesday targeting eight Israeli construction, property development, and architectural firms involved in expanding illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside Tzav 9, an Israeli group that has organized blockades of humanitarian aid entering Gaza. The sanctions include asset freezes and director disqualifications. "Do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution," Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said. The UK said Israel has approved more settlements under its current government than in the previous 20 years. EU sanctions Gaza outlet over alleged Hamas fundraising: The European Union announced new sanctions on Monday against Gaza Now, a Gaza-based social media outlet, and its founder, Mustafa Ayash, accusing them of soliciting funds for Hamas and other armed groups, according to the Associated Press. The sanctions include asset freezes for both the outlet and Ayash, who holds refugee status in Austria and will also face a travel ban across the 27-member bloc. Gaza Now has more than 470,000 followers on X and over one million on Telegram, and was previously sanctioned by the United States in 2024. Yemen Ansarallah reports nine wounded in Sana 'a airstrike: At least nine people were wounded in an airstrike on a shoe factory in the Al-Nahda neighborhood of Sana'a, according to the city's Health Ministry. Ansarallah-affiliated Al-Masirah TV also reported that Saudi airstrikes targeted a demining team in the Kitaf Wa Al-Boqe'e district of Saada governorate. Saudi-backed forces reinforce defenses around Aden amid Ansarallah advance: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces deployed additional troops and military equipment Tuesday around Tur Al-Baha, roughly 85 kilometers (52 miles) from Aden, according to AP. The deployment follows the withdrawal of Saudi-backed forces from positions overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, allowing Ansarallah to consolidate control over the area. Ansarallah has repeatedly denied plans to attack Aden. Saudi Arabia replaces Yemen coalition commander following withdrawal from Bab al-Mandab: Saudi Arabia the commander of its military coalition fighting Ansarallah on Monday, following the withdrawal of Saudi-backed forces from positions near Bab al-Mandab. King Salman appointed General Fayyad Al-Ruwaili to replace Lieutenant General Fahd Al-Salman, who was reassigned as an adviser to the Saudi defense minister, according to Saudi state media. The leadership change follows weeks of Ansarallah advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Saudi-backed forces have struggled to regain territory lost during the offensive, including the key port city of Mocha, while their withdrawal from Bab al-Mandab has allowed Ansarallah to consolidate control near the strait, a critical route for Saudi oil exports amid disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Lebanon Israeli forces continue ceasefire violations across southern Lebanon: Bint Jbeil: Israeli forces the Al-Arish area between the towns of Haris and Hadatha on Tuesday, according to Lebanon's National News Agency. Marjeyoun: Israeli warplanes the town of Houla overnight, while Israeli forces opened fire in Khiam. Nabatieh: Forces shelled Wadi Al-Salouqi and the hills surrounding the towns of Shaqra and Qabrikha at dawn. U.S. envoy urges Hezbollah to disarm voluntarily as UN peacekeeping mandate nears expiration: U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz Hezbollah to voluntarily surrender its weapons to the Lebanese army on Monday. "No country can have two armies. I hope and pray Hezbollah will disarm. They should do that voluntarily," Waltz said. He also said he had met Lebanese leaders to discuss alternatives to the UN peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon, whose mandate expires on December 31. In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement linking Hezbollah's disarmament to a gradual Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon and the deployment of the Lebanese army. Implementation has made little progress amid continued Israeli attacks and occupation of Lebanese territory. U.S. News Hakeem Jeffries moves for recorded leadership vote as Ayanna Pressley flirts with bid: A handful of House Democrats have said recently that they planned to write down the name of Rep. Ayanna Pressley (Mass.) in Wednesday's Speaker contest, relying on the tradition of a secret ballot. Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) subsequently suggested he'll push for a recorded vote, which would make each member's tally public. Jeffries needs 218 votes on the House floor to be elected Speaker. On Monday, Pressley in Boston about the race in the most open terms she had yet, but did not announce an official challenge: "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation when I think about the history of this seat that I occupy--Tip O 'Neill served in this seat, the Speaker of the House; John F. Kennedy served in this seat--this is a historic seat and we have had a historic electoral outcome. We are on the precipice of a historic vote for Speaker and we need to have a historic impact on Congress because that is the decisive mandate by the people, that we move with boldness, not timidity. Scared power isn't power at all. When you have the power you have to use it. Now I am making no declarations or announcements here. What I will say is that I do not need to be the Speaker of the House to speak for the people." Permitting reform clears major Senate hurdle: The Senate moved to end debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) by a 70-27 margin Monday evening, setting it up for final passage. Twenty-one in backing the bill that has the support of both the clean energy and the fossil fuel industries. Its cornerstone provision aims to massively expand transmission capacity, the lack of which is a fundamental obstacle to the buildout of clean energy, but which can also be used to transmit dirty energy. Some environmental advocates whose approach leans more heavily on litigating against energy projects--clean and dirty alike--argued Congress should wait until Democrats control both chambers and can write a better bill. Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey , the lead Senate sponsor of the Green New Deal resolution, delivered a Monday against the bill. The bill's backers counter that the approach ignores the reality that the legislation needs the signature of President Trump and, unless the filibuster is removed, at least some support from Republican senators. Passing BAAJA during the lame duck, meanwhile, would not bar the next Congress from working on improving it. Forensic scientist argues that evidence strongly points to Epstein homicide: Forensic scientist Michael Freeman has begun the findings in his year-long inquiry into Jefferey Epstein 's death, saying Epstein's injuries are most plausibly explained by homicidal strangulation. Freeman, who studies bias and error in death investigation, based his analysis on the autopsy file, given to him by Epstein's brother Mark Epstein. He claims the photos show fingernail marks above the ligature, evidence of neck abrasion and a deep shoulder hemorrhage, all of which point to struggle. His findings have been rejected by scientific journals so far, and some forensic pathologists agree the mark was atypical but say the images could still fit suicide. The New York City medical examiner's office says "it stands by its determination" of suicide. GOP Rep. DesJarlais concedes his reelection race in Tennessee: Tennessee GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais to Democrat Victoria Broderick on Monday in an unexpectedly close race to represent Tennessee's 4th District. Decision Desk HQ has not projected a winner, with Broderick leading 48.87% to 48.73% (a lead of just over 200 votes). She won despite being heavily outspent in a district Trump carried by 24 points in 2024. DesJarlais has served eight terms in Congress. Rep. Ro Khanna suggests $1,700 refund checks for every American to cover costs of Iran War: Rep. Ro Khanna(D-Calif.)** $1,700 refund checks for every American to reimburse Americans for the economic costs of the Iran War, arguing the checks would compensate for higher gas, food, and electricity prices from war-related oil transport disruptions. He urged the House and Senate to pass the proposal in the first week of January ("let's put it on Trump's desk"). Moody's Mark Zandi estimates the war has cost households an average of $2,000. White House tells agencies federal employees "must obtain approval" before agreeing to testify before Congress: In a Monday memo to agency general counsels, Politico reported, White House counsel Will Scharf agency personnel "must obtain approval" from the White House Offices of Legislative Affairs and Counsel before appearing at congressional committees. The directive comes a week after Scharf warned incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia that Democratic investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality," as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Trump, his family, and business interests next year. Commerce and Justice Departments defend handling of Megaspeed: The Commerce and Justice Departments issued a rare joint statement defending their handling of Megaspeed, the Singapore chip buyer at the center of Nvidia's alleged spy scandal, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce of failing to stop Nvidia's sales to the firm. Citing "inaccurate information circulating in public reporting," the statement said Commerce opened a probe in 2024 and that DOJ now leads a criminal case. They did not explain why Megaspeed was never blacklisted. President Trump said Monday that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "might have delayed" doing so to avoid "a blow-up with China." Trump also cast doubt on the spy allegations against Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang , whose affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang forced his resignation last week: "I don't know that she's a spy. Nobody's proven that," while adding that he "wouldn't mind" Huang returning. The turmoil sent Nvidia down 4.1% Monday and dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 2.5% ahead of the company's quarterly earnings after the bell Tuesday. Major software outage at Chase Bank: A software bug at JPMorgan Chase online banking and Zelle transfers for thousands of customers at several major U.S. banks on Monday. A Chase spokesman said Monday the issue was "a software bug in an on-premise hardware system--it is not cyber-related," with other banks affected "only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us." Zelle's owner, Early Warning Services, said its network was fully operational. The disruption followed a Thursday Microsoft outage, Friday's FAA ground stop, and a United Airlines system outage Monday that delayed departures. 📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill? Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com. Other International News UN report: Drone strikes account for over 80% of civilians killed in Sudan in first half of 2026: Drone strikes have come to be a "defining feature" of the war in Sudan, accounting for more than 80% of the civilians killed in the first six months of 2026, according to a new by the UN Human Rights Office. The report documents the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure, indiscriminate attacks, and the continued use of sexual violence as a weapon of war. At least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January until the end of October, with the actual civilian casualty figures likely to be higher, the report found. Civilians in the Kordofan region were the most heavily impacted, accounting for more than two-thirds of documented civilian casualties, followed by the Darfur region, where most of the remaining casualties occurred. "The findings in our report provide more evidence, if any were needed, of the ceaselessly unbearable civilian suffering of the war in Sudan and the warring parties' continued and brazen disregard for the laws of war," UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said. Prominent Bahraini human rights activist dies at 62: Nabeel Rajab, a prominent Bahraini human rights activist who helped lead the country's 2011 pro-democracy protests and spent years in prison for advocating political freedoms and freedom of expression, died Tuesday at the age of 62. His wife and daughter found him unresponsive at their home in Istanbul, Turkey. Rajab, a co-founder and former president of the Bahrain Center for Human Rights, was repeatedly arrested following the Saudi-backed crackdown on Bahrain's 2011 uprising. He was sentenced to five years in prison over social media posts criticizing the Saudi-led war in Yemen, before being released to home detention in June 2020. Rajab left Bahrain earlier this year amid a renewed crackdown on protests following the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the Associated Press that he feared arrest following Bahraini authorities torture of an imprisoned activist. Rajab devoted his final years advocating for Palestinian rights. In one , he shared footage of the destruction in Gaza, writing, "How will the people of this land, which has been reduced to rubble, and their future generations ever forgive our silence, whether we are governments or ordinary people?" Five European countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands Monday they would send rejected asylum applicants to Rwanda as early as next year, Al Jazeera reported. The joint announcement noted that the arrangement is still being negotiated. Rwanda's interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said arrivals could return home, integrate in Rwanda, or move to another country where they can legally reside, claiming that the mechanism would employ an "independent monitoring mechanism" and cooperate fully with UNHCR. Germany's interior minister said it differs from the scrapped 2022 UK deal, which the UK Supreme Court ruled unlawful because Rwanda was not a safe third country, because only those whose claims are rejected would be sent. Forty-seven aid, union, and rights groups urged the countries to abandon the scheme, saying it accepts "the risk of serious human rights violations," and Human Rights Watch said it would provide additional resources to Rwanda's government, which it accuses of serious abuses. Nigeria 's military says it is receiving U.S. intelligence and satellite help in strikes on militants: Nigeria is getting real-time U.S. intelligence and satellite support to target militant leaders ahead of January elections, its defense minister Gen. Christopher Musa Monday, according to Reuters. Musa said troops killed several terrorist and bandit leaders in overnight operations in the northwest and northeast, aided by U.S. satellite imagery, intelligence sharing, and training, and that it is awaiting more helicopters from the U.S. and Italy. He also said Nigeria has agreed a 5-kilometer cross-border "right of pursuit" arrangement with Cameroon, Niger and Chad. Boko Haram and ISWAP attacks on military positions have surged in recent weeks, the military claims, ahead of a January election in which President Bola Tinubu seeks a second term. Mongolian president announces his resignation after accusations of corruption: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa his resignation on Tuesday after the opposition Democratic Party accused him and several top officials in his ruling Mongolian People's Party of corruption. In announcing his resignation he said he would "be investigated and will have my honor restored." He has been president since 2021, and parliament's 126-member State Great Khural must approve his resignation. Costa Rican journalist shot dead in capital: Camilo Rodriguez, who published allegations against suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot and on Monday afternoon on a highway outside San Jose. Attorney General Carlo Diaz said the scene resembling a contract killing and was likely linked to his reporting, adding that Rodriguez had reported threats but declined protection. Rodriguez is the first known journalist killed in Costa Rica in 25 years. Russian strikes two Kyiv bridges hours after Ukraine holds new talks on ending the war: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy online discussions Monday with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and representatives of France, Germany, Britain, Italy, and Poland. He called the discussions "not easy," and noted that parties agreed to meet in Berlin with the "Coalition of the Willing." In Kyiv, Russian strikes hit the North and South bridges over the Dnipro, the city's mayor reported on Monday evening. Two people were killed and the bridges were closed. Separately, Ukraine struck the Crimea Bridge overnight and targeted oil refineries, killing two people near the bridge. name: Andrew Sypher, Turning Point USA
subject: This is exactly what Charlie warned about
body:
I’m going to be blunt with you.

| | |
---
| | Friend,
---
I'm going to be blunt with you.

We are closer to losing this country than most people are willing to admit.

Not someday. Not "if things keep going this way."

Right now.

And the scariest part?

It's not happening in Washington. It's happening in classrooms.

High schools. Colleges.

Places where the next generation is being shaped -- or more accurately... reshaped.

If you've ever looked at what's coming out of our schools and thought: _" What happened to this country?" _

You're not wrong. You're seeing it clearly.

Because while most people are arguing online... while they're hoping things will turn around... while they're waiting for the next election to fix everything...

The other side is doing something far more dangerous.

They're raising the next generation.

Earlier. Faster. And with zero resistance in most places.

That's how countries are lost.

Slowly. Then all at once.

But here's the thing that should give a patriot like you hope...

There is one place where that trend is actually being challenged.

_And it shouldn 't even exist. _

**Just one year ago, Turning Point USA 's high school program -- which is now called "Club America" -- was in about 1,200 schools.**
That alone felt like a miracle.

Because starting even ONE chapter today takes courage most adults don't have.

Conservative students get mocked. Targeted. Threatened. Shut down.

And yet...

_They stepped up anyway. _

About that time, Charlie called me.

He didn't sound optimistic... He sounded urgent.

"Andrew, we've got to move faster."

I told him we were. He stopped me.

"No. You're not thinking what I'm thinking. I want to be in 35,000 high schools."

There is a phrase in politics that needs to disappear: **" Wait your turn."** We hear it all the time. Someone considers running for office, and immediately the political establishment starts asking questions. Whose turn is it? Who has been around the longest? Who has paid their dues? Who has the right connections? Who has already been promised the opportunity? But I have a different question: **Who is best prepared to serve the people?** Public office was never supposed to be an inheritance. It isn't a reward for attending enough political dinners, writing enough checks, or waiting patiently enough for somebody ahead of you to move out of the way. Our government belongs to **We the People**. And if good, qualified, principled Christian conservatives feel called to serve, we should be encouraging them to prayerfully consider running--not telling them to get back in line.

We hear it all the time. Someone considers running for office, and immediately the political establishment starts asking questions. Whose turn is it? Who has been around the longest? Who has paid their dues? Who has the right connections? Who has already been promised the opportunity? But I have a different question: Who is best prepared to serve the people? Public office was never supposed to be an inheritance. It isn't a reward for attending enough political dinners, writing enough checks, or waiting patiently enough for somebody ahead of you to move out of the way. Our government belongs to We the People. And if good, qualified, principled Christian conservatives feel called to serve, we should be encouraging them to prayerfully consider running--not telling them to get back in line. ? # [Patriotism Is More Than Just What We Defend](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=4399133&post_id=225357026&utm_source=post-email-title&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjI1MzU3MDI2LCJpYXQiOjE3OTQ5MzIxMzYsImV4cCI6MTc5NzUyNDEzNiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTQzOTkxMzMiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.zIsIuOLxM2KkAwk2-Jyr6HYGnsu3y1kbqVc-cksHK3k)
### It's about what we build - From the GI Bill to America's defense industrial base, the economic case for investing in the next generation of veterans.
| | [Patrick J. Murphy](https://substack.com/@patrickmurphypa) and [Genine Fallon](https://substack.com/@g9fallon)

American politicians may disagree about nearly everything, but they have found a rare point of consensus when it comes to rebuilding our industrial strength. From factories and semiconductor plants to shipyards and power grids, both parties have embraced the urgency of creating good-paying jobs and strengthening domestic manufacturing so our defense industrial base can keep up.
There is just one problem. We can't rebuild America's industrial might without the skilled workers needed to make it happen. Enter the American veteran. Every year, roughly 200,000 service members leave the military and enter civilian life.
America has been here before. Some of our greatest periods of progress have been shaped by what veterans did after they came home. The World War II generation helped build the modern American middle class, thanks in part to the opportunities created by the GI Bill, but also to the ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of veterans who went on to build iconic American companies like Walmart, Lowe's, and Enterprise Rent-A-Car. Later generations followed, with veterans helping build brands like Nike and Ralph Lauren. Vietnam veterans did the same. Marines like Fred Smith and Bob Parsons came home and founded FedEx and GoDaddy.
Our generation has a different challenge ahead: helping America rebuild the industries and infrastructure that will support its economy for decades to come. Nearly half of World War II veterans went on to start their own businesses, compared with fewer than 5% of post-9/11 veterans, according to historical estimates. We need to do more to ensure that the skills, experience, and entrepreneurial spirit of those who served continue to benefit our country long after they leave the military.

## **The GI Bill and the Creation of the American Middle Class**
When World War II ended, more than 16 million Americans had served in uniform. The country faced an enormous question: How would millions of returning service members find jobs, buy homes, and build lives after the war?
The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, better known as the GI Bill, helped answer that question. It paid for college and vocational training and offered government-backed loans that made it easier for veterans to buy homes and start businesses.
The GI Bill helped millions of veterans enter the middle class while supplying American businesses with the skilled workers they needed during the postwar boom. And contrary to how we often think about the program today, college was only one of several paths it offered. More veterans pursued vocational and technical training than traditional higher education.
But the GI Bill's benefits were not shared equally. Discrimination in lending, housing, and educational access prevented many Black veterans from receiving the same opportunities as their white counterparts.
For all its shortcomings, the GI Bill helped establish a powerful precedent of investing in veterans.
## **Vietnam Veterans and A New Commitment to Those Who Serve**
When Vietnam veterans came home, they returned to a country deeply divided over the war they had fought. Our nation didn't separate the war from the warrior. Instead of the welcome many had hoped for, some encountered hostility, shame, and a stigma that followed them long after they took off their uniforms. Others carried invisible wounds that went unrecognized for years, struggling to get the medical care and support they desperately needed.
But rather than accept those failures, Vietnam veterans organized to change how America treated its service members. They fought for recognition of post-traumatic stress disorder, demanded accountability for Agent Orange exposure, and pushed for better healthcare and benefits.
Vietnam Veterans of America adopted a motto that captured their determination: "Never again will one generation of veterans abandon another."
That commitment represented a remarkable act of grace. Many Vietnam veterans had experienced the consequences of a country struggling to reconcile its political divisions with its obligations to those who served. Rather than allowing those experiences to define the treatment of future veterans, they devoted decades to building stronger institutions and a more durable national commitment to military families. They were the first to say "Welcome Home Brother" or "Welcome Home Sister" to our Iraq and Afghanistan veterans.
Where World War II veterans helped build America's postwar economy, Vietnam veterans helped change how America cares for those who serve.
## **The Post-9/11 Generation and the Economics of Veteran Transition**
The United States now faces workforce shortages that present an opportunity for veterans entering civilian life.
The country is seeking to expand domestic manufacturing, modernize infrastructure, strengthen supply chains, and maintain technological leadership in areas including artificial intelligence, advanced materials, energy systems, and defense production. These priorities depend on the availability of skilled workers across construction, transportation, industrial maintenance, manufacturing, and technical occupations.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects substantial annual openings across many of these fields over the coming decade, driven by both employment growth and the need to replace retiring workers. Workforce constraints can delay capital projects, increase operating costs, reduce manufacturing capacity, and weaken the ability of American businesses to compete.
Meanwhile, roughly 200,000 service members transition from active military service into civilian life annually. Many have spent years operating sophisticated equipment, managing complex logistics, maintaining technical systems, leading teams, and making decisions in demanding environments.
The Pentagon has spent years and billions of dollars training them. Yet when they return home, some discover that their military qualifications don't count toward the civilian licenses or certifications they need. Others struggle to explain their experience to employers unfamiliar with military occupations. A veteran who could maintain a multimillion-dollar aircraft may still have to start from scratch to qualify for a civilian job.
A more effective approach would treat veteran transition as part of a broader workforce development strategy, aligning military experience, education benefits, employer requirements, and regional economic priorities.
The relevant measure of success should extend beyond initial employment placement. Sustainable career progression, earnings growth, and financial stability provide a more meaningful assessment of whether transition programs are delivering value.
## **Visiting Unlimited Human Potential**
On Veterans Day last week, in the shadows of the world's largest global retailer - Walmart - in Bentonville, Arkansas, we visited Unlock Human Potential (UHP) for their annual gala, where Army Special Forces veteran/founder Matt Hesse is working to help veterans turn the skills they've developed in uniform into rewarding civilian careers.
_Here 's a sizzle reel of UHP:_
[](https://substack.com/redirect/eb8fbec5-5d1b-4080-852e-e6de876ec24b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Matt's vision is grounded in the idea that the military's methods of developing talent--intensive training, practical application, structured accountability, and team-based learning--can inform a more effective model for preparing veterans for civilian careers.
UHP combines accelerated technical education with human performance and community. Its six industrial training areas include electrical work, welding, commercial driving, advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, and culinary arts. Three additional disciplines focus on nutrition, health coaching, and personal training.
The organization reports operating on approximately 800 acres with $50 million in infrastructure and has outlined plans to increase residential capacity from a baseline of 280 beds to 1,000. Its expansion strategy identifies Pennsylvania, Virginia, Nevada, and Florida, with reported corporate relationships including Walmart, Salute, Lockheed Martin, Raytheon, Apple, BILT, Primo Brands, and Crossland.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/cc112b2b-8844-4b4f-b74d-71569ca43a08?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Patrick and Genine with Hattie Douglas, U.S. Air Force veteran.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/339274e4-2d2e-4a4e-bea6-717e919685f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Patrick speaking at the UHP gala.
These figures represent organizational plans and, to date, have a 100% success rate. We sat through some of the instruction, and the model's long-term value will be evaluated through recognized credentials, graduation rates, employment placement, earnings, retention, and the cost of achieving those outcomes - but early days show Matt's vision coming to fruition big-time.
What makes the vision significant is its potential application beyond one institution. Accelerated training programs aligned with regional workforce demand could help reduce the time between military separation and productive civilian employment while maintaining the community and structure that support successful transitions.
## **Walmart and the Private Sector 's Role in Veteran Economic Mobility**
Sam Walton is the WWII Army veteran who legendarily came home and started building Walmart. But he passed down his servant's heart and entrepreneurial spirit to his son [John Walton](https://substack.com/redirect/ecde9f4d-5e96-488f-8147-1c045b03bf2a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), who went on to serve as a Green Beret in Vietnam. Employers and veterans each have an integral role in converting military experience into civilian economic opportunity, and Walmart provides an example of the scale at which private-sector engagement can operate.
Since 2013, Walmart has reported hiring more than 500,000 veterans and military spouses, including more than 30,000 veterans in fiscal year 2026. The company has also adopted a skills-first approach to workforce development, with more than 90 percent of its U.S. roles not requiring a four-year degree.
The significance of this approach extends beyond the number of veterans hired. It reflects an employment model that places greater emphasis on demonstrated capabilities and transferable skills, rather than relying exclusively on conventional academic credentials.
The next stage of private-sector engagement should focus on deeper integration between employers, training providers, and military transition programs. Employers can help identify emerging skills requirements, participate in curriculum development, recognize relevant credentials, and establish clearer pathways from training to employment.
When structured effectively, veteran employment initiatives should make companies "vet-ready," not merely "vet-friendly," as part of an organization's talent strategy rather than a separate corporate philanthropy effort.
## **Modernizing the GI Bill for America 's Next Industrial Era**
The original GI Bill demonstrated how investments in veterans could contribute to broader economic transformation.
The next opportunity is to ensure that these benefits remain aligned with the changing structure of the American economy.
The GI Bill already supports approved vocational and technical schools, apprenticeships, and on-the-job training. The policy challenge is therefore not to introduce skilled trades into the program, but to improve access to rigorous, accelerated, industry-aligned pathways while maintaining strong protections for veterans and taxpayers.
Three areas deserve particular attention.
**First, modernize access to accelerated training.** Approval requirements and benefit structures should be evaluated to determine whether they appropriately accommodate intensive, short-duration programs that lead to recognized credentials and employment in high-demand industries. Program quality and accountability must remain central to eligibility.
**Second, strengthen outcome-based accountability.** Enrollment and completion rates provide only partial measures of success. Policymakers should also evaluate credential attainment, employment placement, earnings growth, retention, and career progression. These measures would help distinguish programs delivering sustainable economic value from those generating credentials without meaningful labor-market outcomes.
**Third, integrate veteran transition with regional workforce strategies.** The Department of Defense, Department of Veterans Affairs, Department of Labor, employers, labor organizations, and training providers should coordinate more closely to connect military experience with regional economic needs. Service members should have clearer information about career opportunities, recognized credentials, and training pathways before leaving military service.
These reforms would not diminish the importance of traditional higher education. Four-year degrees remain valuable pathways for many veterans. However, a modern education benefits system should recognize that economic opportunity can also be created through apprenticeships, technical certifications, skilled trades, and accelerated training programs.
## **The Responsibility of Our Generation**
The history of American veterans demonstrates that the value of military service cannot be measured solely by what happens during a period of conflict.
The World War II generation helped create the foundation for decades of economic expansion, supported by a GI Bill that invested in education, technical training, homeownership, and entrepreneurship. Vietnam veterans helped establish stronger institutions and a more enduring national commitment to those who serve, demonstrating grace and civic responsibility at a time when the country had struggled to extend the same understanding to them.
The Post-9/11 generation now has an opportunity to contribute to another defining national priority: strengthening America's economic and industrial future.
Realizing that opportunity will require more than expressions of gratitude or isolated employment initiatives. It will require coordinated investment in human capital, more effective alignment between education benefits and labor-market demand, and sustained partnerships among government, employers, and training institutions.
We should evaluate the success of these investments over decades rather than months. The original GI Bill invested $14.5 billion in educational benefits and studies show the return on investment resulted in $7 to $12 in economic returns through increased productivity, higher lifetime earnings, and elevated tax revenues.
The original GI Bill demonstrates what becomes possible when America views its veterans as an investment in national prosperity. Eight decades later, that principle remains relevant to the country's most pressing economic challenges.
As we reflect on this past Veterans Day, the responsibility is not simply to recognize what previous generations sacrificed, but to consider how our generation can now contribute to our country's future.
Patriotism isn't just about defending America. It's about building it.

Marines like Fred Smith and Bob Parsons came home and founded FedEx and GoDaddy. Our generation has a different challenge ahead: helping America rebuild the industries and infrastructure that will support its economy for decades to come. Nearly half of World War II veterans went on to start their own businesses, compared with fewer than 5% of post-9/11 veterans, according to historical estimates. We need to do more to ensure that the skills, experience, and entrepreneurial spirit of those who served continue to benefit our country long after they leave the military. The Secretary's SitRep is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. The GI Bill and the Creation of the American Middle Class When World War II ended, more than 16 million Americans had served in uniform. The country faced an enormous question: How would millions of returning service members find jobs, buy homes, and build lives after the war? The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, better known as the GI Bill, helped answer that question. It paid for college and vocational training and offered government-backed loans that made it easier for veterans to buy homes and start businesses. The GI Bill helped millions of veterans enter the middle class while supplying American businesses with the skilled workers they needed during the postwar boom. And contrary to how we often think about the program today, college was only one of several paths it offered. More veterans pursued vocational and technical training than traditional higher education. But the GI Bill's benefits were not shared equally. Discrimination in lending, housing, and educational access prevented many Black veterans from receiving the same opportunities as their white counterparts. For all its shortcomings, the GI Bill helped establish a powerful precedent of investing in veterans. Vietnam Veterans and A New Commitment to Those Who Serve When Vietnam veterans came home, they returned to a country deeply divided over the war they had fought. Our nation didn't separate the war from the warrior. Instead of the welcome many had hoped for, some encountered hostility, shame, and a stigma that followed them long after they took off their uniforms. Others carried invisible wounds that went unrecognized for years, struggling to get the medical care and support they desperately needed. But rather than accept those failures, Vietnam veterans organized to change how America treated its service members. They fought for recognition of post-traumatic stress disorder, demanded accountability for Agent Orange exposure, and pushed for better healthcare and benefits. Vietnam Veterans of America adopted a motto that captured their determination: "Never again will one generation of veterans abandon another." That commitment represented a remarkable act of grace. Many Vietnam veterans had experienced the consequences of a country struggling to reconcile its political divisions with its obligations to those who served. Rather than allowing those experiences to define the treatment of future veterans, they devoted decades to building stronger institutions and a more durable national commitment to military families. They were the first to say "Welcome Home Brother" or "Welcome Home Sister" to our Iraq and Afghanistan veterans. Where World War II veterans helped build America's postwar economy, Vietnam veterans helped change how America cares for those who serve. The Post-9/11 Generation and the Economics of Veteran Transition The United States now faces workforce shortages that present an opportunity for veterans entering civilian life. The country is seeking to expand domestic manufacturing, modernize infrastructure, strengthen supply chains, and maintain technological leadership in areas including artificial intelligence, advanced materials, energy systems, and defense production. These priorities depend on the availability of skilled workers across construction, transportation, industrial maintenance, manufacturing, and technical occupations. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects substantial annual openings across many of these fields over the coming decade, driven by both employment growth and the need to replace retiring workers. Workforce constraints can delay capital projects, increase operating costs, reduce manufacturing capacity, and weaken the ability of American businesses to compete. Meanwhile, roughly 200,000 service members transition from active military service into civilian life annually. Many have spent years operating sophisticated equipment, managing complex logistics, maintaining technical systems, leading teams, and making decisions in demanding environments. The Pentagon has spent years and billions of dollars training them. Yet when they return home, some discover that their military qualifications don't count toward the civilian licenses or certifications they need. Others struggle to explain their experience to employers unfamiliar with military occupations. A veteran who could maintain a multimillion-dollar aircraft may still have to start from scratch to qualify for a civilian job. A more effective approach would treat veteran transition as part of a broader workforce development strategy, aligning military experience, education benefits, employer requirements, and regional economic priorities. The relevant measure of success should extend beyond initial employment placement. Sustainable career progression, earnings growth, and financial stability provide a more meaningful assessment of whether transition programs are delivering value. Visiting Unlimited Human Potential On Veterans Day last week, in the shadows of the world's largest global retailer - Walmart - in Bentonville, Arkansas, we visited Unlock Human Potential (UHP) for their annual gala, where Army Special Forces veteran/founder Matt Hesse is working to help veterans turn the skills they've developed in uniform into rewarding civilian careers. Here 's a sizzle reel of UHP: Matt's vision is grounded in the idea that the military's methods of developing talent--intensive training, practical application, structured accountability, and team-based learning--can inform a more effective model for preparing veterans for civilian careers. UHP combines accelerated technical education with human performance and community. Its six industrial training areas include electrical work, welding, commercial driving, advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, and culinary arts. Three additional disciplines focus on nutrition, health coaching, and personal training. The organization reports operating on approximately 800 acres with $50 million in infrastructure and has outlined plans to increase residential capacity from a baseline of 280 beds to 1,000. Its expansion strategy identifies Pennsylvania, Virginia, Nevada, and Florida, with reported corporate relationships including Walmart, Salute, Lockheed Martin, Raytheon, Apple, BILT, Primo Brands, and Crossland. | | ---|---|--- Patrick and Genine with Hattie Douglas, U.S. Air Force veteran. | | ---|---|--- Patrick speaking at the UHP gala. These figures represent organizational plans and, to date, have a 100% success rate. We sat through some of the instruction, and the model's long-term value will be evaluated through recognized credentials, graduation rates, employment placement, earnings, retention, and the cost of achieving those outcomes - but early days show Matt's vision coming to fruition big-time. What makes the vision significant is its potential application beyond one institution. Accelerated training programs aligned with regional workforce demand could help reduce the time between military separation and productive civilian employment while maintaining the community and structure that support successful transitions. Walmart and the Private Sector 's Role in Veteran Economic Mobility Sam Walton is the WWII Army veteran who legendarily came home and started building Walmart. But he passed down his servant's heart and entrepreneurial spirit to his son , who went on to serve as a Green Beret in Vietnam. Employers and veterans each have an integral role in converting military experience into civilian economic opportunity, and Walmart provides an example of the scale at which private-sector engagement can operate. Since 2013, Walmart has reported hiring more than 500,000 veterans and military spouses, including more than 30,000 veterans in fiscal year 2026. The company has also adopted a skills-first approach to workforce development, with more than 90 percent of its U.S. roles not requiring a four-year degree. The significance of this approach extends beyond the number of veterans hired. It reflects an employment model that places greater emphasis on demonstrated capabilities and transferable skills, rather than relying exclusively on conventional academic credentials. The next stage of private-sector engagement should focus on deeper integration between employers, training providers, and military transition programs. Employers can help identify emerging skills requirements, participate in curriculum development, recognize relevant credentials, and establish clearer pathways from training to employment. When structured effectively, veteran employment initiatives should make companies "vet-ready," not merely "vet-friendly," as part of an organization's talent strategy rather than a separate corporate philanthropy effort. Modernizing the GI Bill for America 's Next Industrial Era The original GI Bill demonstrated how investments in veterans could contribute to broader economic transformation. The next opportunity is to ensure that these benefits remain aligned with the changing structure of the American economy. The GI Bill already supports approved vocational and technical schools, apprenticeships, and on-the-job training. The policy challenge is therefore not to introduce skilled trades into the program, but to improve access to rigorous, accelerated, industry-aligned pathways while maintaining strong protections for veterans and taxpayers. Three areas deserve particular attention. First, modernize access to accelerated training. Approval requirements and benefit structures should be evaluated to determine whether they appropriately accommodate intensive, short-duration programs that lead to recognized credentials and employment in high-demand industries. Program quality and accountability must remain central to eligibility. Second, strengthen outcome-based accountability. Enrollment and completion rates provide only partial measures of success. Policymakers should also evaluate credential attainment, employment placement, earnings growth, retention, and career progression. These measures would help distinguish programs delivering sustainable economic value from those generating credentials without meaningful labor-market outcomes. Third, integrate veteran transition with regional workforce strategies. The Department of Defense, Department of Veterans Affairs, Department of Labor, employers, labor organizations, and training providers should coordinate more closely to connect military experience with regional economic needs. Service members should have clearer information about career opportunities, recognized credentials, and training pathways before leaving military service. These reforms would not diminish the importance of traditional higher education. Four-year degrees remain valuable pathways for many veterans. However, a modern education benefits system should recognize that economic opportunity can also be created through apprenticeships, technical certifications, skilled trades, and accelerated training programs. The Responsibility of Our Generation** The history of American veterans demonstrates that the value of military service cannot be measured solely by what happens during a period of conflict. The World War II generation helped create the foundation for decades of economic expansion, supported by a GI Bill that invested in education, technical training, homeownership, and entrepreneurship. Vietnam veterans helped establish stronger institutions and a more enduring national commitment to those who serve, demonstrating grace and civic responsibility at a time when the country had struggled to extend the same understanding to them. The Post-9/11 generation now has an opportunity to contribute to another defining national priority: strengthening America's economic and industrial future. Realizing that opportunity will require more than expressions of gratitude or isolated employment initiatives. It will require coordinated investment in human capital, more effective alignment between education benefits and labor-market demand, and sustained partnerships among government, employers, and training institutions. We should evaluate the success of these investments over decades rather than months. The original GI Bill invested $14.5 billion in educational benefits and studies show the return on investment resulted in $7 to $12 in economic returns through increased productivity, higher lifetime earnings, and elevated tax revenues. The original GI Bill demonstrates what becomes possible when America views its veterans as an investment in national prosperity. Eight decades later, that principle remains relevant to the country's most pressing economic challenges. As we reflect on this past Veterans Day, the responsibility is not simply to recognize what previous generations sacrificed, but to consider how our generation can now contribute to our country's future. Patriotism isn't just about defending America. It's about building it. The Secretary's SitRep is a reader-supported publication. _" That's just not true!" _

* * *
# Breaking headlines:
# **Trump warns Iran of severe retaliation if alleged DC attack plot is launched**
### _**" We take it very seriously"**_
President Donald Trump **[warned Iran would"pay a price](https://substack.com/redirect/0d21250a-933f-490a-b820-bb0067d62c80?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** the likes of which no country has ever paid before" if it attacked Washington, D.C., responding to a CNN report that Iran is reportedly weighing a chemical weapon or dirty bomb attack targeting senior administration officials, though officials say the plot remains preliminary.
[| | | | | CBS News
---
@CBSNews
President Donald Trump said the U.S. is taking seriously reports of a potential Iranian plot to detonate a "dirty bomb" in Washington, D.C., when asked about the alleged threat on Tuesday. Trump warned that Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid ...
| 12:34 PM * Nov 17, 2026 * 28.2K Views51 Replies * 28 Reposts * 74 Likes
---](https://substack.com/redirect/be0710fd-e1e6-4622-b7a8-524aa6815600?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
* **Trump made the comments while in the Philippines** meeting with QUAD leaders, and said he plans to press Chinese President Xi Jinping this week to help end the Iran war; the White House maintains there's no credible imminent threat to the homeland.
* **The report follows news that several top officials,** including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and War Secretary Pete Hegseth, have relocated to military housing amid Iranian assassination threats and broader domestic security concerns.

* * *
# **DHS Secretary Mullin downplays tech outages, rules out cyberattack**
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin **[assured Americans the country remains secure](https://substack.com/redirect/98917808-cbca-4feb-b2d1-b7726a978e32?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** following widespread disruptions to banks, airlines, and Microsoft services, saying with "98% certainty" the incidents weren't connected or linked to a cyberattack.
* **Outages hit Chase, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, and Bank of America Monday,** following a Friday FAA ground stop and a separate Microsoft outage last week; JPMorgan Chase said its issue wasn't security-related and customers retained access to funds.
* **Mullin suggested aging infrastructure is struggling to keep pace with newer technology,** and relayed a tech expert's theory that AI "super intelligence" self-correcting code could have triggered cascading effects across systems not built to handle its speed, calling the explanation plausible.

* * *
# **BREAKING: Cyberattack reportedly hits 178 major websites including CNN, Fox News**
Researchers at Report URI **[identified malicious code affecting 178 organizations,](https://substack.com/redirect/0eee08bd-e819-4616-b3f3-41ac0a927350?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** including Zoom, BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, Salesforce, and Fox News, after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's website testing platform rather than breaching each company individually.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/0eee08bd-e819-4616-b3f3-41ac0a927350?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **The injected code attempted multiple forms of theft,** including redirecting cryptocurrency payments, stealing credit card details, accessing browser-stored information, and capturing screenshots, with some code also targeting vulnerabilities in older iPhone and iPad software.
* **Optimizely said it has fixed the vulnerability, removed the malicious code,** secured affected accounts, and added new protections, though the company continues monitoring the incident. Researchers traced roughly $7,040 in cryptocurrency transfers to wallets linked to the attack, though the full financial impact remains unknown.
* **Visiting an affected site alone doesn 't confirm compromised data, but** anyone who entered payment or cryptocurrency details on November 16 should update devices, review bank and crypto transactions, watch for suspicious account activity, and report unauthorized charges to their bank.

* * *
# **FEMA to conduct nationwide emergency alert test Tuesday**
FEMA's legally required Emergency Alert System **[test will air across radio, TV, cable, and satellite providers](https://substack.com/redirect/0f7476f1-3778-4a9f-b85c-7cf5c7363eb8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** around 2:20 p.m. ET for roughly one minute, broadcasting a standard "this is only a test" message with no action required.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/0f7476f1-3778-4a9f-b85c-7cf5c7363eb8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **The agency addressed online speculation ahead of time,** clarifying via social media that the drill is routine and unrelated to recent tech outages affecting banks, airlines, and other services that have fueled public anxiety.
* **Unlike the 2023 test, this one won 't send alerts to cell phones,** focusing solely on broadcast systems; a backup date of December 3 is set if an actual emergency disrupts Tuesday's scheduled test.

Unlike the 2023 test, this one won 't send alerts to cell phones, focusing solely on broadcast systems; a backup date of December 3 is set if an actual emergency disrupts Tuesday's scheduled test. Lower costs, protect care, and defend lifesaving research. | |
**Peter, one of my first priorities in Congress will be reversing the devastating Medicaid cuts and protecting access to health care.**

I recently joined Peter Alexander on _State of Play_ to talk about the rising cost of living and why no one should have to choose between paying their rent and getting the health care they need. Protecting health care also means protecting the scientific research that makes lifesaving treatments and medical breakthroughs possible.

That's why I authored a $7.5 billion science bond in California, which will go before voters in March 2028, to help protect critical research from federal funding cuts.

Scientific research is helping us prevent and cure diseases, develop new treatments, and improve the lives of people living with chronic conditions.

We cannot allow federal cuts to undermine that progress or put future medical breakthroughs at risk.

**There is so much work ahead of us to make health care more affordable, accessible, and effective for everyone. As I prepare to take on these fights in Congress, I want to hear directly from you.

A clip is making the rounds this week under a caption that does more damage than any media-criticism op-ed could: "Journalism 101 at MIZCOMO." The footage is old -- Stephen Miller, back when he was a White House policy aide, sparring with CNN's Jim Acosta in the briefing room -- but the caption is brand new, posted the same week Miller settles into the chief of staff's office. The joke writes itself, which is precisely the problem. The internet watched a political operative dismantle a network correspondent's question and decided the moment amounted to basic training. Not for Miller. For the press.

It's a standard tactic among politicians running for federal office. When you don't have anything else to campaign on, yell about lazy, do-nothing civil servants. "And if I'm elected, I will take your mandate to Washington to cut the civil service to the bone!" Pause for applause.
One of the very few who actually tried it was Bill Clinton.
Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
[Pledge your support](https://substack..sRrAp5-sXTmYN5swoRyM4Cb0bnmw0EKT5xy33xq8scc?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=225372628)
With the Cold War over, Clinton felt the federal workforce needed change. Two years later, and with Congress's support, he signed the Federal Workforce Restructuring Act of 1994, which reduced the federal workforce by nearly half a million people. Everyone, even the civil servants, had to admit the process had worked.
But Clinton never denigrated the value of civil service workers. He started the process by saying, "We will turn first to Federal employees for help. They know better than anyone else how to do their jobs if someone will simply ask them and reward them for wanting to do it better."
Civil servants provide expertise that cannot be replicated. I routinely worked with people who had thirty years of experience and were the smartest in their fields. Civil servants can be conservative and cautious in the face of change; bureaucratic conservatism often blunts fresh political appointees' desire to come in and make their mark quickly, before they have had a chance to understand the true impact of their decisions. The protection of the Civil Service Acts also guaranteed that civil servants could give an honest assessment without worrying about their jobs... well, at least it used to be that way.
Jump to 2025. Donald Trump has just been inaugurated. He campaigned on a near-hatred of government workers. One of his first actions was to illegally create the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and illegally appoint a non-government employee, Elon Musk, to run it. Trump gave Musk unlimited, extra-legal powers to fire any government employee he saw fit. DOGE began firing people capriciously, without warning and without any logical basis. Courts overturned these firings again and again; they found that nearly all of Musk's actions were illegal, but damage was done. The FAA and air safety are a prime example.
Trump started with a commission that President Biden appointed in 2023 to recommend upgrades to America's air traffic control system. Trump disbanded the commission as soon as he took office.
Then, three weeks after a tragic accident over the Potomac River, four hundred FAA employees, many in radar maintenance and aviation safety, were informed by a late Friday night email that their employment had been terminated. In the weeks that followed, another 1,300 took early retirement. Both the Professional Aviation Safety Specialist union and the Air Traffic Controllers Association warned that this would significantly affect aviation safety and airline operations, but the cuts went ahead.
We saw the impacts last week. For the first time since 9/11, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, canceling tens of thousands of flights. Sean Duffy, the Secretary of Transportation and former MTV reality TV star, has tried to tell us that while upgrading the air traffic control system, a contractor in Arkansas was plugging a fiber-optic cable into a router, and the next thing you know, nobody was flying anywhere.
I have no idea whether that explanation is true, but here's one thing I do know. The civil servants, the group with the expertise to manage the massive job of upgrading our air traffic control systems, are largely gone. This would have left the program to contractors focused on completing the job quickly to maximize profits, and to inexperienced political appointees focused only on speed to gain recognition.
So, the next time you hear a political candidate say the federal civil service is the root of so many problems in the federal government, remind them that before DOGE fired tens of thousands of experienced civil servants, you didn't have to wait two days for your flight.
**THE NEWS YOU NEED TO SEE**
**Alabama Political reporter:**_**" Alabama Arise warns proposed SNAP rule could increase hunger"**_
The Department of Agriculture is proposing a policy change that will cut SNAP benefits for millions of people. The change will prohibit states from extending SNAP income limits to families receiving other forms of assistance. Opponents say it will push more people into food insecurity. The USDA acknowledges that the policy will remove 6.5 million people from SNAP rolls, but it will save $45 billion... the cost of one unnecessary war with Iran.
[https://www.alreporter.com/2026/11/17/alabama-arise-raises-alarm-regarding-proposal-to-limit-snap-eligibility](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/18193a0d-c7c3-4a1c-aebe-e0497222f061?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**Farm Action:**_**" Rancher Prices Fall Nearly 20% Amid Trump's Beef Import Plan"**_
As predicted, Trump's plan to import tens of thousands of tons of beef from Argentina has devastated America's cattle farmers. Trump did it to try to bring down prices in the run-up to the mid-term elections. That clearly didn't work.
[https://farmaction.us/rancher-prices-fall-nearly-20-amid-trumps-beef-import-plan/?fbclid=IwY2xjawVoQflleHRuA2FlbQIxMABwZG9mAWJyaWQRMUJlYll4STE3Vjlyc2VTbmJzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEfRI-6DdusjcdF4nrbI6nLijnTC609RIbHB8zgT12nJzwjZd0vze7q18xPqPA_aem_FjRehzpcE2sq0dW9Z6Nfqg](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/299e16e9-5985-46da-91b8-6f793f77ad2f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**Yellow Hammer News:**_**" Defense industry gives its highest honor to Mike Rogers for 'dogged determination'"**_
In the least surprising news of the week, the National Defense Industrial Association awarded the 2026 Dwight D. Eisenhower Award to Mike Rogers (R-Lockheed Martin) for his "dogged determination" to double the defense budget no matter the need. The irony is that in his farewell address to the nation, President Eisenhower said, "In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist."
[https://yellowhammernews.com/defense-industry-gives-its-highest-honor-to-mike-rogers-for-dogged-determination/](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/f0802671-2a71-4b98-8f2d-b568917bbe38?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

With Election Day officially in our rearview and the new slate of Democrats preparing to get sworn into office, it’s time to start thinking about how we want to govern.

Voters gave us a mandate, folks, and voted for Democrats in record numbers across the state.

## **Grand Theft Crazy: What Washington and Parents Need to Wake Up To**
Today on Capitol Hill, the Senate Judiciary Subcomittee on Crime and Counterterrorism is convening a groundbreaking bipartisan hearing on the massive online gaming platform Roblox - and what millions of American children are actually being exposed to behind closed bedroom doors.
[| | | | | CBS News
---
@CBSNews
Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.
| | cbsn.ws
---
Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of first-ever congressional hearing on the issue
| |
| 7:03 PM * Nov 16, 2026 * 26.7K Views8 Replies * 14 Reposts * 58 Likes
---](https://substack.com/redirect/f8dd9719-4186-40fc-bc2a-befaa5fed739?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Most parents and grandparents know Roblox simply as that popular game their kids are constantly asking for money to play.
What families don't realize is what is lurking inside that platform. Beyond the inappropriate content accessible inside user-created spaced, the ability for predators and unknown adults to reach out directly to young children has become a massive, growing crisis - one that has already sparked nearly 200 federal lawsuits.
**Yet as alarming as the Roblox hearing is, we are about to hit an entirely new level of concern this Thursday when** _**Grand Theft Auto VI**_**launches.**
Analysts are already projecting billions of dollars in opening sales and a $2 billion hit to the U.S. economy from millions of workers expected to call out sick on release day.
**But the lost productivity isn 't even close to the real problem. **
What this game is going to allow players to do - and what millions of underage kids across America are about to treat as normal, everyday entertainment - should alarm every single parent, leader, and citizen in this country.

### November 17, 2026 Newsletter
---
| | Supervillains Beware! Peachy Keenan Is Here!
---
| [](https://momsforamerica.us/so/34Q7fhLrh/c?w=EO5sCqCOd1KGSA0ieP_DfLxvZY3AZOWabhx2pF7lp3c.)

| | Who are the supervillains shaping today's culture, and how are their ideas influencing the world around us? Peachy Keenan returns to the Moms for America Podcast after her lively conversation about Domestic Extremist, this time bringing her signature humor and fearless commentary to Supervillains, a satirical look at the people, movements, and ideologies reshaping American culture. With sharp wit and plenty of laugh-out-loud observations, Peachy shines a light on the cultural craziness we see unfolding around us. But beyond the humor is an important conversation about recognizing the forces influencing our families, challenging the ideas that threaten our values, and standing strong for what matters. It's time to pull back the curtain, call out the absurdities, and remember that we don't have to sit back and watch culture happen. Join us for a fun, thought-provoking conversation with Peachy Keenan! Find the Moms for America Podcast on all your favorite platforms [YouTube](https://momsforamerica.us/so/34Q7fhLrh/c?w=rjdFEq6cF4X4BK35pCGu0NNvNF0ggP3fpn2DktsEX1Y.), [Rumble,](https://momsforamerica.us/so/34Q7fhLrh/c?w=kSxPz0NBk2bLn_9-VzrT1doJchfV5c7_cdKk5SAjME8.eyJ1IjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ydW1ibGUuY29tL2MvYy0xMjA2NzMzP2U5cz1zcmNfdjFfY2JsIiwiciI6IjlhYWYzNDE2LTljNTYtNGYxOC04ODUwLWNkZDcwZGM4Nzg0YiIsIm0iOiJtYWlsIiwiYyI6ImIzODM4YmY4LWZhYjAtNDFiOS05NjczLWU4YzZiZWZiNjU3NyJ9) [Spotify](https://momsforamerica.us/so/34Q7fhLrh/c?w=v4AJtm_qsYjDD0_2lWJRpP3QMBizMbWvbka6jNtDaRk.), and [Apple](https://momsforamerica.us/so/34Q7fhLrh/c?w=rpRWuUtUkJbuk3h8O30uwMZe-Oa9u6hjqdpdM5cE-vo.).
